reading.title: How to Use Sources in a Report
reading.purpose: Learn the tools writers use to find facts, share them fairly, and let readers check them.
paras: A good report begins with research, which means studying a topic carefully to find facts. Where should you look? Start with a reference, such as an encyclopedia or a dictionary, that you use to look up facts. Then add books and articles written by experts.

As you read, look for the passage that answers your question. A passage is a short section of a book or an article. Use a marker to highlight the important words, but do not color the whole page. When you want to use someone's exact words, copy only an excerpt, a short piece from the longer text, and put it in quotation marks. A quotation is the exact words of a speaker or writer.

Sometimes the best proof is a document, such as a letter, a map, or an official form that serves as a record. Records from long ago can be very valuable because they show what people wrote at the time.

Your readers should be able to check your facts. A footnote is a short note at the bottom of a page that explains an idea or names a source. A bibliography is a list of the books and sources you used, usually in alphabetical order. A glossary, a list of hard words and their meanings, can help readers who meet an unfamiliar term.
Writing from sources takes patience, but it makes your report trustworthy. Readers believe you when they can see exactly where each fact came from.

choices: a short note at the bottom of a page that explains an idea
a list of hard words with their meanings at the back of a book
a short section of a book that answers one question
a list of the sources you used

qs.q: Which sentence tells how to show someone's exact words in a report?
choices: Use a marker to highlight the important words, but do not color the whole page.
When you want to use someone's exact words, copy only an excerpt, a short piece from the longer text, and put it in quotation marks.
A passage is a short section of a book or an article.
Start with a reference, such as an encyclopedia or a dictionary, that you use to look up facts.
qs.why: This sentence says to copy a short piece and put it in quotation marks.

ev.text: When you want to use someone's exact words, copy only an excerpt, a short piece from the longer text, and put it in quotation marks.

qs.q: Why might a reader doubt a report that has no footnotes or bibliography?
choices: The reader cannot check where the facts came from.
The reader will find too many hard words in the text.
The reader will think the report is much too short.
The reader will not know who highlighted the pages.
qs.why: Footnotes and a bibliography name the sources, so without them readers cannot check the facts.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: A report should copy a whole article so nothing is left out.
Highlighting every sentence is the fastest way to learn.
Good reports name their sources so readers can check facts.
An encyclopedia is the only source a writer may ever use.
qs.why: The reading shows how to find, quote, and name sources, and ends by saying this makes a report trustworthy.
